title: Who Checks Whether a Cleanup Held?
hook: The EPA remediated 13,000 Omaha yards and moved on. Reporters retested 620 of them for $10 a sample — and found lead above the agency's own trigger in four of every ten.
key_points: Omaha's 27-square-mile lead Superfund site, created after a smelter closed in the 1990s, is the largest residential lead site in the US.
The EPA remediated over 13,000 properties by December 2015, handed remaining work to the city, and does not typically retest.
ProPublica sampled soil at 620 homes over two years, using single samples analyzed by an EPA-accredited lab at about $10 each.
41% of yards citywide exceeded 100 ppm — a level an EPA model links to elevated blood-lead in children; over half of 390 yards inside the site did.
One in ten of 150 already-remediated yards topped 400 ppm, the EPA's original cleanup threshold.
Recontaminated yards clustered beside untreated lots, suggesting contaminated soil migrates from properties the cleanup skipped.
content_html: Environmental regulation has a follow-up problem. Agencies are organized to do cleanups — assess a site, treat it, sign off — and much less well organized to ask, years later, whether the treatment held. ProPublica's testing in Omaha put a number on that gap.
extra_html:
Omaha's Superfund site covers 27 square miles, designated after the American Smelting and Refining Company's operations closed in the 1990s left more than a century of lead deposition; it is the largest residential lead Superfund site in the country. The EPA began testing in 1999 after elevated blood-lead levels turned up in children, remediated more than 13,000 residential properties by December 2015, then transferred the remaining work to the city. What it does not do is retest — so residents who want current data generally have to pay for it.

So reporters did the testing. Over two years they collected soil from 620 homes, taking a single sample of three or four tablespoons from the middle of each yard with a sterilized spoon, away from houses and roads, and sending them to an EPA-accredited lab at roughly $10 apiece. Forty-one percent of yards citywide came back above 100 parts per million, a level an EPA model associates with elevated blood-lead in children; inside the Superfund boundary, more than half of 390 yards exceeded it. Among 150 yards the EPA had already remediated, about one in ten topped 400 ppm — the threshold that triggered the original cleanup — and those clustered near properties that were never treated, pointing to soil migrating from untreated lots. The EPA criticized the single-sample method as potentially biased high or low, while outside experts told ProPublica that enough single samples do support broad conclusions about an area; the agency said it would look into the findings and work with Omaha under its 2009 cleanup guidance. The transferable lesson is about institutional design rather than lead: a program that funds remediation but not verification is telling you how much it spent, not what it achieved.

related.title: Environmental Governance
related.hook: How do you regulate something that ignores borders and belongs to no one? Environmental governance is the toolkit societies use to manage nature collectively.

related.title: From Local Investigation to Federal Policy, in Two Months
related.hook: A local newsroom's investigation found California let dozens of teachers accused of sexual misconduct keep working. The federal government cited it directly when it acted.

related.title: Accountability & Oversight
related.hook: Power left unwatched drifts toward abuse. Accountability is the demand that officials answer for what they do — and oversight is the machinery that makes them.

related.title: The Tragedy of the Commons
related.hook: When everyone shares a resource but no one owns it, each person's rational choice can add up to collective ruin. That trap explains a huge slice of environmental politics.

flashcards.prompt: Why does a completed environmental cleanup not settle whether the site is safe?
flashcards.back_html: Because nobody is required to check again. Remediation is verified when the work is done; without retesting, later recontamination — for instance from untreated neighboring lots — goes unmeasured.

flashcards.prompt: What did ProPublica's soil sampling find in Omaha yards that had already been remediated?

choices.text: About 1 in 10 of the 150 tested exceeded 400 ppm, the EPA's original cleanup threshold
All of them exceeded the original cleanup threshold

flashcards.explanation_html: Remediated yards were not immune: roughly a tenth were back above the 400 ppm level that triggered cleanup in the first place, clustering near untreated lots.

flashcards.prompt: The EPA objected that single soil samples could be 'biased high or low'. What was the response?

choices.text: Experts said single samples support broad conclusions about an area when enough are collected
The samples were discarded and never analyzed
The EPA's own composite method was shown to be invalid

flashcards.explanation_html: The disagreement is about methodology, not results: one sample per yard is noisy for one yard, but 620 of them characterize a neighborhood.
